strengths: Generating a virtual correspondence from point coordinates and then reusing five-point and P3P solvers is an original, useful simplification of a difficult geometric problem. The training-free centroid variant is particularly attractive because it achieves competitive results with little implementation complexity. This supported contribution provides the main case for weak acceptance.

The experiments provide meaningful evidence on 10,000 real image triplets. In Table 1, the learned solver improves AUC@5° over the homotopy-continuation baseline from 43.25 to 47.14 on Sacre Coeur and from 19.45 to 21.34 on St. Peters’ Square. The centroid solver performs close to that baseline. Training the learned variant entirely on synthetic data also provides useful evidence of transfer to real imagery.

The evaluation includes noise sensitivity, classical baselines, and informative oracle comparisons. The supplementary two-view experiment on 9,900 image pairs supports applicability beyond three-view estimation: the centroid variant takes 0.03 seconds versus 0.04 for five-point estimation, with a modest AUC@5° reduction from 63.71 to 61.48.

The manuscript clearly acknowledges the overconstrained nature of 4p3v, the approximation error on noiseless inputs, and the strong performance of the existing five-point-plus-P3P baseline. The supplementary architecture, loss, synthetic-data generation, and training settings help reproducibility. The contribution retains value despite not outperforming that classical baseline overall.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not fully measure three-camera geometry. Section 5 scores Sampson residuals and rotation/translation-direction errors only for pairs 1–2 and 1–3. These quantities cannot detect an incorrect relative baseline scale, an identifiable component of the joint three-camera pose. Baseline-ratio error, pair 2–3 geometry, or reconstruction error after a common similarity alignment would be needed to substantiate complete three-view accuracy.

The efficiency advantage is limited. In Table 1, the learned solver takes 38.50 and 14.13 seconds versus 2.08 and 1.83 seconds for homotopy continuation. Five-point-plus-P3P generally matches or exceeds its accuracy while being substantially faster. The centroid variant has comparable, slightly worse accuracy and slightly longer runtime than homotopy continuation. The evidence therefore establishes implementation simplicity more convincingly than an improved accuracy–runtime tradeoff.

The operating range of the centroid approximation remains insufficiently characterized. The triangle-radius bound in Section 3.3 does not establish that virtual matches fall within useful inlier thresholds, and Figure 2 reports average behavior rather than error tails or successful-hypothesis probabilities. Figures 3–4 demonstrate persistent noiseless bias. Without controlled outlier-ratio experiments or analysis across perspective distortion and depth variation, the suggested benefit from smaller RANSAC samples remains unverified.

Reproducing the robust-estimation results requires details absent even from the supplement: inlier thresholds, stopping confidence and iteration limits, handling of multiple five-point/P3P solutions, and the local-optimization procedure. These choices matter when comparing solvers with different approximation errors and failure rates. Code and trained models are promised, but their availability is not established in the supplied manuscript.
